entry.title: Task info slots 4 and 5 are a write and skip pair
entry.summary: Two virtual slots overridden by every task info class turned out to be a matched pair: one writes the object's field values into a network bit stream, and the other walks the same bit layout without storing anything. Naming all 150 functions in the batch took the high-confidence count to 6 and medium to 131, with 13 left unnamed.
entry.content:
Two virtual slots overridden by every task info class turned out to be a matched pair: one writes the object's field values into a network bit stream, and the other walks the same bit layout without storing anything. Naming all 150 functions in the batch took the high-confidence count to 6 and medium to 131, with 13 left unnamed.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what each address group is about first and grading every name high, medium or low confidence.

What was found

Verified Slot 6 of the task info classes was already proven to serialize fields into a network bit stream. Slot 4 reads the object's own fields by value and passes them to bit-stream helpers, and one override writes computed zero padding in a loop, which only makes sense in the write direction.

Inferred Slot 5 replays the exact bit-count sequence of the matching slot 6 but passes no field values, writes no memory in any of its 33 overrides, and discards every intermediate result. The only reading that fits all of that is advancing past the task's data, so it was named skip rather than read.

Verified The bit-stream helpers both slots call sit in the encrypted code range and decode as garbage, so their roles were derived from caller-side shapes only. Five more published names in that range turned out to be shared-stub mislabels on decode, including two called by these very overrides.

Verified The rest of the batch held a camera factory with a 42-way type switch, nine single-type camera finders, render-phase render and state-copy virtuals, interior instance constructors and destructors, and a streaming cluster with a make-space retry loop, entry admission gate, slot acquisition and fragment-list handling.

What was decided or recommended

Slot 4 overrides were named write task data and slot 5 overrides skip task data at medium confidence, with the read-versus-skip reasoning recorded per function so a lane with a decrypted image can confirm it in minutes. Vague setters and thin wrappers whose purpose could not be determined were left unnamed rather than given placeholder names.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each task info slot 4 and slot 5 override from the mapped executable image, list the direct-call targets and memory writes per override, and compare the helper and bit-count sequence of each slot 5 against the same class's slot 6 serialize override. Direct callers were found with a whole code-section scan for call instructions.

What was confusing or went wrong

The slot 5 direction took most of the lane: read, skip and write-defaults all fit the first few overrides, and only the fully worked comparison against slot 6 plus the unwritten scratch argument settled it. A disassembler output quirk hid small push constants from the evidence table, and shell output redirection wrote an unreadable text encoding, both of which cost a re-run each.

entry.title: Naming a run of task info functions
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty unnamed functions turned out to be the task descriptor subsystem, and nearly all of them were named from their vtables plus a factory that maps task ids to constructors.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty unnamed functions turned out to be the task descriptor subsystem, and nearly all of them were named from their vtables plus a factory that maps task ids to constructors.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each, working out what the group is about first.

What was found

Verified About three quarters of the batch sit in vtables whose classes are recoverable from runtime type records, and every task info vtable uses the same four slots.

SlotBehaviour seenName given
read slotreads fields bit by bit from a buffer after calling the base readerdeserialize
print slotprints state lines through one shared line printer after the base linesappend_debug_info
size slotadds a per-class constant to the base valueget_serialized_size
name slotmaps a status number to its name string via a jump tableget_status_name

Verified One large function switches on the task id and constructs the matching task info object, which identifies unknown task ids for the whole batch.

Verified Eight small entries are not functions: one is jump-table data and seven are switch case arms only reachable through jump tables.

What was decided or recommended

Shared vtable bodies are named with the class the slot-vector diff points at: inherited bodies take the base class, while byte-identical bodies shared by unrelated classes are recorded as linker folds with every sharer listed. Later lanes should diff full slot vectors before naming any shared body, and should treat tiny relocation-only entries as switch arms until a real caller turns up.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image, collect per-function callees, referenced strings and data cross-references into one table, group data references into vtables, decode each vtable class from its runtime type record, then confirm each slot role by reading a few members closely and checking every other member matches the same call pattern.

What was confusing or went wrong

Four near-identical entity resolvers looked like one function copied four times until their bytes showed different field offsets, one per task info class. A type record read at the wrong offset returned truncated class names until the correct field was used. Two existing slot labels in the merged names picked the wrong class for shared bodies, corrected here by inheritance diffs.

entry.title: One clone factory forgot its null check, and two contract traps that hid branches
entry.summary: Rewriting forty small task-system routines showed three things worth keeping: one clone routine crashes where its eight siblings return cleanly, equal pin periods can silently untest a branch, and a script period can lock against the fill rotation and hide a copied byte. All forty were verified with wrong versions that fail.
entry.content:
Rewriting forty small task-system routines showed three things worth keeping: one clone routine crashes where its eight siblings return cleanly, equal pin periods can silently untest a branch, and a script period can lock against the fill rotation and hide a copied byte. All forty were verified with wrong versions that fail.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty small game routines in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the checker, one contract per routine, at least a thousand trials each, and a deliberately wrong version per routine that must fail.

What was found

Verified The batch is one family: constructors, destructors, deleting destructors, clone factories and poll predicates for the complex-task system, all sharing one heap singleton and a few global slots.

Verified One of nine clone routines has no null check after allocating. Its eight siblings return a null pointer on allocation failure; this one keeps going and writes through null, which faults. The rewrite reproduces the fault exactly, so two thirds of trials pass normally and one third match fault for fault.

Verified One factory calls the allocator from two places, one per kind. A contract that patched only one site ran the real allocator bytes on the other path and faulted there, failing exactly the share of trials that take that path.

Verified Pins that all cycle with the same period can leave a combined path unrunnable: in one list-scanning predicate the tag-hit combination never occurred, so the first wrong version passed every trial. Mixed periods fixed it.

Verified Heap fills rotate in threes across trials, so a three-step answer script can sit in fixed phase with them. In the byte-copying clone this left the interesting trials on fills where source and destination bytes were equal, and the wrong version passed until the script phase was shifted.

What was decided or recommended

  • Collect every call site per callee before writing patches; a fault share equal to a branch share points at a missed site.
  • When several pins gate one path, prove the joint schedule covers it; equal periods are guilty until proven innocent.
  • Keep three-step scripts off phase with the fill rotation whenever the proof observes copied bytes.
  • The missing null check looks latent (the real allocator presumably never returns null) and was reproduced rather than fixed.

How to reproduce it

Generate one contract per routine with a script, asserting each patch site against the executable first; build all rewrites plus their wrong versions in one small crate; run each contract for a thousand trials on the stock checker and confirm the wrong version fails within its short run. The lane notes in the scratch folder name the generator and the exact fixes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The allocator fault was confusing at first: the failing trials looked like wild-pointer parity until the fault share matched the kind branch exactly, which pointed at the second call site. The two passing wrong versions were also surprising in sequence; both turned out to be inputs that never reached the changed behaviour rather than checker gaps, and both were fixed by rescheduling inputs, not by touching rewrites.

entry.title: Naming a run of task sync, camera and vehicle functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three clean families: per-class task network-sync virtuals whose four slots each have one fixed meaning, a camera-chain search and link family, and vehicle model setup including spawn color selection. 139 got names, 11 stayed unnamed.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three clean families: per-class task network-sync virtuals whose four slots each have one fixed meaning, a camera-chain search and link family, and vehicle model setup including spawn color selection. 139 got names, 11 stayed unnamed.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with a confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first. No rewriting, no checker: names only, with evidence ranked from strings and imports down to observed reads and writes.

What was found

Verified The largest family is task-info network sync: dozens of classes each override the same four virtual slots. One slot serializes the info fields into the network bit stream and chains to its parent override, one builds a task for a given ped, one builds a task from the stored info fields, and one builds a default task ignoring them. The last two were told apart inside a single class: both call the same task constructor, one with the info byte, one with constant zero. A big id-keyed factory constructs the matching info subclass per id.

Verified The camera family walks two chains of cam nodes using one virtual slot as a type id, with countdown matching, plus attach, copy and flag helpers. One startup function builds the heap that the camera deleting destructor frees back to.

Verified The vehicle group holds model load and unload virtuals, a flag-string parser, a matched pair that loads and releases the shared vehicle texture dictionary, and three color-combo selectors sharing one table set: sequential advance, random avoiding current, and a spawn picker that scans nearby same-model vehicles and maximizes color distance from them.

Inferred The inventory subsystems for most of this range are address-cluster artefacts; the functions belong to tasks, cameras and vehicles instead. Four inventory sizes overrun into the next function, one size-zero entry is not a function, and one real destructor between two entries has no entry at all.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the slot meanings for the task family, the chain roles for the camera family, and observed behaviour elsewhere. Trivial getters, flag helpers with unknown bit semantics, and jumps to unknown helpers were left unnamed rather than given vague names. The next lane in a task-info range can reuse the four slot meanings directly; the destructor at the gap between two listed entries needs its own entry.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the memory-mapped image indexed by relative address, never the raw file at a mapped address, and decode one known function end to end first: the first attempt here decoded garbage and the check caught it. Gather per-function callees resolved against the merged symbol tables, exact-start string references only, and caller lists from a text-wide direct-call scan, then read the short functions and one member per family fully. Map vtable addresses stored in destructor bodies to classes through the class-hierarchy files.

What was confusing or went wrong

Substring string matching produced floods of false hits; only pointers to the exact start of a string were kept. Nearest-symbol call-site attribution spills across missing function starts, so large offsets lie about the caller. Several inherited names turned out to be wrong, including a shared encrypted-range stub labelled as a helicopter method and a message-send native, and a generic container free labelled as a timing detach. The base-class task-info slots live in the encrypted range, so their meanings had to be derived from the plaintext overrides instead.

entry.title: A wrong-code backend bug, caught by the checker
entry.summary: A production lane rewriting small streaming-subsystem functions found a miscompile in the release compiler: a correct Rust rewrite of a table lookup failed differential testing because the compiled code dropped part of its own result expression. Pinning one value with an optimizer barrier fixed it, and the fixed rewrite verified over one thousand trials.
entry.content:
A production lane rewriting small streaming-subsystem functions found a miscompile in the release compiler: a correct Rust rewrite of a table lookup failed differential testing because the compiled code dropped part of its own result expression. Pinning one value with an optimizer barrier fixed it, and the fixed rewrite verified over one thousand trials.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty small game functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, one thousand trials per function, each with its own deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified Thirty-three of the forty functions verified with full default comparison and every wrong version caught. Seven were deferred: four pass pointers to their own stack frame into callees, three call through registers or tables.

Verified One rewrite failed forty of sixty probe trials even though its source was a faithful transcription: the low result byte always matched and the high bits were always zero. Disassembly of the lane's own freshly built rewrite library showed the backend had compiled (index & mask) | flag to just the flag load, discarding the masked index. The same pure expression gives the right answer when built for the host machine, and a minimal two-function reproduction shows the trigger: the folded-away value must also be used as the index of the flag's own table load. A barrier call on that value produces the full mask-and-or sequence and the rewrite then passes.

Verified Two contract-authoring traps bit during the lane. First, per-address global values replace the blanket random fill entirely, so a large table range combined with one fixed pointer silently stayed zero and made a wrong version pass sixty of sixty; explicit random words for the whole range fixed it. Second, a three-entry scripted-answer list aliases with the fill rotation (zeros, pattern, random by trial modulo three), so one callee's heap path never saw random bytes and its wrong version passed; four-entry lists decorrelate them.

What was decided or recommended

The affected rewrite keeps the barrier call with a comment pointing at the lane report, and the minimal reproductions are filed with the lane for a future compiler bug report. Later lanes should keep every cycling list length coprime to three unless the correlation is deliberate, and should spell out random words for any range combined with fixed global values.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's rewrite crate for the 32-bit Windows target at optimization level two and disassemble the kind-flag lookup export: without the barrier the final mask-and-or collapses to a zero-extending byte load. The lane's minimal reproduction file shows the same collapse for a parameter-driven variant and the correct sequence with the barrier. The checker mismatch is deterministic: the original returns the scaled index with the flag in the low byte, the miscompiled rewrite returns the flag alone.

What was confusing or went wrong

The miscompile was initially indistinguishable from a rewrite bug: identical inputs, matching low byte, zeroed high bits. What broke the confusion was disassembling the lane's own output instead of re-reading the source. The two contract traps were quieter: both produced passing verdicts that were weaker than they looked, and both were caught only because a wrong version unexpectedly passed, which is exactly the signal the per-function wrong version exists to give.

entry.title: A batch that could not be verified: the code section flaps under us
entry.summary: A production batch of forty small streaming-subsystem functions verified zero times, not because the rewrites were wrong but because the original bytes kept changing: the executable's code section flaps between a decrypted and an encrypted state while its modification time stays frozen.
entry.content:
A production batch of forty small streaming-subsystem functions verified zero times, not because the rewrites were wrong but because the original bytes kept changing: the executable's code section flaps between a decrypted and an encrypted state while its modification time stays frozen.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each identical with the stock checker, one contract per function, one thousand trials each, plus a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified Two reads of the batch range minutes apart were byte-identical and decoded to sensible functions; later reads of the same range decoded to garbage, with the file modification time unchanged throughout.

Verified The checker worker reads the live file faithfully: a three-site worker-versus-local byte comparison agreed on all three sites, and a paired probe late in the lane showed both sides seeing the encrypted byte.

Verified Five full thousand-trial runs each ended with every trial faulting on the original side while the rewrite ran cleanly. Twenty-one further contracts were written and schema-validated but never executed.

Inferred The rewriting writer is none of the usual suspects: the lane writes nothing outside its scratch folder, the checker never writes the executable, and no matching background process was found. Sibling batches verify normally, so the flap is specific to this range and time.

Unknown What performs the rewrite, on what schedule, and when the decrypted state returns.

What was decided or recommended

All decryptable functions were deferred as needing encrypted code, with rewrites and contracts kept for re-run. The durable lesson for other lanes: never gate a run on a local byte read. The lane probed the worker side directly by pointing a patch-site check at the batch range and reading which byte the worker reported; once, a locally confirmed decrypted window still produced encrypted-style faults. Re-run the kept contracts only after the worker itself reports decrypted bytes.

How to reproduce it

Take any validated contract for a function in the affected range and run it for a handful of trials: every trial faults on the original side. Then make a one-trial copy of a known-good probe contract with a patch site aimed into the batch range; the setup report names the byte the worker sees there, which can be compared against a mapped read of the same offset.

What was confusing or went wrong

The disassembly files were written in UTF-16, so a script reading them with the default codec silently matched nothing; the fix was one codec argument. An early relocation check double-added the block address and falsely flagged every absolute read as unrelocated; the entry value already includes the page offset. Per-function minutes in the results file are wall-clock time split evenly, not individually measured, and are labelled as such.

entry.title: Three original-code idioms that need narrowed proofs
entry.summary: Verifying a batch of forty small game functions turned up three patterns in the original code that no rewrite can replicate exactly, each needing an honest narrowing note rather than a fudge.
entry.content:
Verifying a batch of forty small game functions turned up three patterns in the original code that no rewrite can replicate exactly, each needing an honest narrowing note rather than a fudge.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, one thousand trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified Two object initialisers read words from their own uninitialised stack scratch and store them into fields. The values are whatever the stack happens to hold, so the proof defines them as zero and records that.

Verified One function keeps the standard stack-cookie check, whose cookie value is derived from the stack pointer and therefore differs between the original and any rewrite frame. Its early path also returns that cookie. The proof checks the control flow and the check call itself, and excludes the cookie value.

Verified One device-selection routine passes five words to a query callee that leaves them on the stack, pushes two more, and calls a device routine that pops all seven. Reading the pushes alone suggests the wrong argument count; the only consistent accounting pops twenty-eight bytes, and neighbouring functions repeat the same idiom a dozen times.

Verified Two functions return leftovers rather than computed values on some path: one returns its placer's answer with the low byte replaced by a mode test, another reads its level byte after a call that overwrote it with the call's answer. Both were caught by failing trials and then replicated.

What was decided or recommended

Narrowed proofs that say what they exclude are acceptable; the batch finished with thirty-nine verified functions and one deferral. Recommended for other lanes: when a call sequence will not balance, count callee cleanups across neighbouring callers before assuming an argument count; when a rewrite mismatches on one trial only, suspect a missed register clobber before suspecting the checker.

How to reproduce it

Each function's proof contract states its inputs, scripted callee answers and narrowing notes, and its verdict file records one thousand passing trials plus a caught wrong version. The batch list names the forty functions; the lane folder holds the rewrites, contracts, verdicts and the per-function results file.

What was confusing or went wrong

One function failed a single trial out of sixty with both sides logging identical visible call prefixes; the difference hid past the log truncation. A manual single-trial run with full logs showed the original computing zero where the rewrite computed its input, which traced to the overwritten level byte above, not to the checker's per-call answer sequences as first feared. Separately, call-argument skip indexes count from the top of the stack (last pushed), which is the opposite of the order the pushes are read in; two contracts initially skipped the constant and compared the buffer instead of the other way round.

entry.title: Naming batch 88: task slots, RTTI ctors and a full sort family
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions resolved into five groups: vehicle doors and entry, a complete sort routine for frag records, the explosion manager, player tasks, and vehicle model helpers. One hundred and forty got names, fifty-one at high confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions resolved into five groups: vehicle doors and entry, a complete sort routine for frag records, the explosion manager, player tasks, and vehicle model helpers. One hundred and forty got names, fifty-one at high confidence.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred and fifty unnamed functions that sit next to each other in the executable, working out what the group is about first. No rewriting, only names with confidence levels.

What was found

Verified The task system vtable slots now have confirmed meanings: joining every lane-named task method against its inventory slot showed slot zero is the destructor, one is clone, three is the task-type constant, five is make-abortable, seventeen is the simple-task tick, and eighteen, nineteen and twenty are create-next, create-first and control subtask. That join named forty-one functions in this batch.

Verified Four small constructors and two destructors were identified exactly by reading RTTI type names through the executable parser: they belong to the move-in-air, move-player, move-swim and pause-timer task classes. No guessing was needed.

Verified Fourteen functions form one complete standard-library sort for eight-byte records, with the depth-limited quicksort, the insertion-sort finish and the full heap family. Its single caller sorts explosion target pairs and processes each equal-key group with buoyancy and ragdoll updates.

Inferred The first group is labelled input and user interface in the inventory but the code is vehicle doors, seats and entry, including a passenger-ejection loop and a long can-use-vehicle gate. The label looks wrong.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established task vocabulary from earlier naming lanes. Ten tiny predicates and struct fills were left unnamed with low confidence because their owning semantics never surfaced. The slot-meaning join and the RTTI constructor trick are recommended for the naming brief, since together they resolved a third of the batch without reading code instruction by instruction. The simple-task slot thirteen still has no established meaning.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function first: named callees from the merged lane names, referenced strings, and stored vtable addresses resolved to class names through RTTI. Confirm task vtable slots by joining lane names to inventory slots on address. Map sort-family roles by call shape with exact function sizes, not by overrunning disassembly into neighbours. Place opaque leaves with a call-reference scan of the code section.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early call-shape script disassembled a fixed twelve hundred bytes per function and ran into neighbouring functions, producing nonsense edges; exact inventory sizes fixed it. One batch entry overlaps the destructor after it, and one function jumps into the middle of another, so both needed care. The inventory subsystem label for the first group was misleading until the callees made the vehicle theme plain.

entry.title: Two streaming helpers read their own return address
entry.summary: Two small functions in the streaming subsystem consume their own return address as data: one passes its address bits on as a floating-point argument to a helper, the other branches on its low byte. Both were left unverified because no faithful rewrite can reproduce the behaviour.
entry.content:
Two small functions in the streaming subsystem consume their own return address as data: one passes its address bits on as a floating-point argument to a helper, the other branches on its low byte. Both were left unverified because no faithful rewrite can reproduce the behaviour.

What was asked

A production lane rewrote and verified a batch of forty small streaming-subsystem functions against the original with the project checker, one contract per function.

What was found

Verified The batch verified all but six functions. Two of the six share one surprising trait, established by instruction decode and stack accounting, not by guessing:

  • One helper computes a float, stores it into its own argument slot, then loads the float it passes onward from the neighbouring slot — the slot holding its return address. Stack-balance accounting shows its intermediate call cleans nothing itself, which pins the load to the return-address slot on every path.
  • A second helper reads the same slot's low byte after its calls and takes or skips a whole block of work on it, so its control flow depends on a value no caller controls.

Inferred Both look like compiler artifacts (a slot computed for one frame layout, code generated for another) rather than deliberate logic: in the running game the values are whatever addresses the callers happen to return to. Neither crashes; both are deterministic for a given build.

What was decided or recommended

Both functions were recorded as deferred with reason other and a precise description of the mechanism, and their neighbours verified normally. A rewrite would have to read its own entry stack to reproduce either behaviour, which the rewrite language cannot express, so no contract was attempted. Future lanes should treat any function whose decoded frame touches the return-address slot the same way: decode first, and defer rather than approximate.

How to reproduce it

Decode either function from the batch list with capstone through the mapped image (never raw file bytes at a mapped address), count pushes from the entry to each stack reference, and balance the frame both ways for each callee convention. The return-address reads fall out of the arithmetic.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first helper initially looked like an ordinary float computation with a wrong-operand failure; only the frame-balance check, done to rule out a calling-convention mistake, showed the loaded slot sits one word above the stored one. A first triage script also mislabelled four unrelated functions as reading unrelocated globals by assuming every displacement sits at the instruction end; re-done by byte search, all are relocated and all four verified.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard functions verified as one family, plus a checker anomaly
entry.summary: A batch of eight same-sized functions turned out to be one leaderboard routine instantiated eight times, differing only in a small constant, and all eight rewrites passed twelve hundred trials each with their wrong versions caught; while debugging, a rewrite with a wrong call shape passed every completed comparison on the stock checker, which needs a checker-side explanation.
entry.content:
A batch of eight same-sized functions turned out to be one leaderboard routine instantiated eight times, differing only in a small constant, and all eight rewrites passed twelve hundred trials each with their wrong versions caught; while debugging, a rewrite with a wrong call shape passed every completed comparison on the stock checker, which needs a checker-side explanation.

What was asked

Rewrite eight original game functions in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, one contract per function, at least a thousand trials each, plus one deliberately wrong version per function that the checker must reject.

What was found

Verified The eight functions share one body: the same callees at the same relative positions, the same two object-table calls, the same loop over nineteen ranks, differing only in one leaderboard identifier constant. A generator asserts that shape for every member and emits all contracts and rewrites.

Verified Each function collects leaderboard rows: it reads a selected rank through the object, looks a rank table up through a frame buffer, classifies each rank through a small switch, and either copies the selected payload or places rows against a cursor, setting one mask bit per placed rank. The callee takes the cursor from before the stride is added, a detail the first rewrite got wrong and the checker caught.

Verified All eight passed twelve hundred trials with zero failures, none vacuous, every declared callee fired, and every wrong version (a stride constant changed by half) rejected through the call comparison. Three narrowings apply to all eight and are recorded in the verdicts: the stack comparison is off because the original spills two values into dead argument slots, one frame-buffer address is skipped and snapshotted instead of compared, and only the low return byte is compared.

Verified A rewrite that passed two stack arguments to a three-argument callee, corrupting the stack pointer on every such call, passed twenty-six of twenty-six completed trials with zero failures on the stock checker across three identical runs. The verdict failed only because a later trial crashed the worker process.

ObservationStatusMeaning
Wrong call shape passes completed trials on stockverified, three runscomparisons saw no difference where one must exist
Same-argument value change is rejected on stockverified controlthat argument is compared in the value case
Same inputs fail on a source-built workerverified controlstock and source-built workers diverge on identical inputs
Why the stock runs passunknownneeds a checker-side investigation, not a lane guess

What was decided or recommended

  • The eight verifications stand: they are positive proofs with balanced calls and rejected wrong versions, and the anomaly needs a stack-corrupting rewrite to show itself.
  • The anomaly is preserved as a runnable repro in the lane folder (a small buggy crate, one contract, two probe verdicts, and a private worker whose only change is an append-only call log), so the checker owner can re-run it directly.
  • Two smaller asks: worker-lost trials currently leave the failure count at zero with no mismatch shown, which reads like a pass; and the stock worker binary postdates its source file by minutes, so binary-versus-source drift should be ruled in or out.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's buggy crate and run the stock checker driver on the probe contract for sixty trials: expect zero comparison failures until one trial crashes the worker and aborts the run. Then run the same probe with a worker built from the tracked source: expect about a third of the trials to fail with the rewrite faulting. A companion probe that changes one argument value instead of the argument count fails promptly on the stock worker, confirming the comparison works in that case.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Two self-inflicted bugs cost the most time: passing the cursor after instead of before the stride was added, and an edit that silently dropped one call argument. The second one produced a deterministic worker crash that first looked like machine flakiness under load; disassembling the lane's own build showed the missing argument.

Verified An early relocation scare (jump tables looking unrelocated) turned out to be a script bug reading the relocation table with doubled offsets; a corrected check showed every table fully relocated, so no special checker ability was needed.

Unknown The anomaly mechanism itself: every readable part of the stub and comparison says the mismatched call must fail, yet the stock runs pass. This stayed unknown after controls and a private-worker dump, and is reported as unknown rather than guessed at.

entry.title: Naming a batch of 150 functions: bound helpers, cull pipelines, ped intelligence
entry.summary: A naming batch of 150 consecutive unnamed functions turned out to hold three code families, and all 150 were named with 13 at high confidence, 134 at medium and 3 deliberately left empty.
entry.content:
A naming batch of 150 consecutive unnamed functions turned out to hold three code families, and all 150 were named with 13 at high confidence, 134 at medium and 3 deliberately left empty.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive project-style name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each, working from strings, imports, known callers and callees, vtables and class layouts rather than rewriting anything.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three families in order: composite bounding-volume helpers operating on a four-array object with counts, active flags and capped id lists; visibility, placement and attach pipelines including frustum clipping in three variants, a timing-slot table and ped-mount solvers; and ped-intelligence methods including the constructor, destructor and several table and entry helpers.

Verified Two merged script-native labels were wrong and were caught by reading call sites: one suspected message-sending native is an operator-delete style free function called from a deleting destructor, and one suspected bomb-placement native is a table-store helper called with a slot index. Five draft names written on the first wrong label were corrected.

Verified One zero-size inventory entry is not a function but the tail of the preceding destructor, and two entries are pure jump thunks, one of which was resolved through a double jump to a global-table reset.

What was decided or recommended

High confidence is given only for vtable slots, verified-rewrite callees or layouts, and semantics read directly from the code. Low-confidence merged native labels should be treated as hints until a call site confirms them. A later lane should identify the exact class of the composite-bound object, which has no known vtable.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: disassemble through the mapped executable image, collect direct calls, import calls and string references per function, scan for callers and data references once, and look every callee up in the verified rewrites, lane names and merged symbols. Then read the short functions fully and the large ones by head, tail and call flow, and write the names file incrementally.

What was confusing or went wrong

The wrong native labels cost about fifteen minutes of euphoria-themed draft names before a destructor call pattern exposed the free function. A raw-byte caller scan overcounts callers because the call opcode byte also appears inside other instructions, so its counts are upper bounds only. Time felt much shorter than the machine clock showed, which nearly caused a rushed finish.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed until the contract was widened
entry.summary: A deliberately wrong version of a global-vector append function passed one hundred trials out of one hundred, which showed that the checker's global-memory comparison could not see which word of a multi-word range had changed.
entry.content:
A deliberately wrong version of a global-vector append function passed one hundred trials out of one hundred, which showed that the checker's global-memory comparison could not see which word of a multi-word range had changed.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of small streaming-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the checker, giving every function its own deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified The wrong version stored its value one slot too far and still passed every trial. Reading the checker's comparison code showed why: when a declared global range holds several words, every changed word is recorded under the range's base address rather than its own, so two writes of equal values in equal order compare equal no matter which words they hit. Declaring each word as its own range restored the check, and the wrong version then failed as required.

Verified Earlier accepted rewrites that only read globals, or write a single global word, cannot be affected by this gap; only multi-word global writes were blind.

What was decided or recommended

The lane's multi-word global contracts were rewritten with one word per range, and all affected functions were re-verified with their wrong versions failing. The recommended checker fix is to record each changed global word under its own address, exactly as the check for undeclared writes already does.

How to reproduce it

Take any function that writes two words of one declared global range, write a variant that swaps which word gets which value, and run both against the same contract: before the fix the variant passes; with one word per range it fails.

What was confusing or went wrong

The passing wrong version first looked like a mistake in the variant itself, and only reading the comparison code turned it into a checker finding. The same batch also produced an unsolved fault at an indirect stub call, deferred with the evidence, and several batch sizes that end mid-instruction and had to be re-decoded by hand.

entry.title: Production batch: four task functions verified, one dead descriptor found
entry.summary: All four functions in this batch were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact against the original over 1200 trials each, and one of them turned out to initialise a descriptor it never uses while handing its callees an uninitialised frame slot.
entry.content:
All four functions in this batch were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact against the original over 1200 trials each, and one of them turned out to initialise a descriptor it never uses while handing its callees an uninitialised frame slot.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring task-system functions (467 to 1657 bytes each) in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version 5 checker, including a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All four rewrites pass 1200/1200 trials with bit-exact float comparison, and all four wrong versions are caught.

Verified The configuration function's visible six-word descriptor initialisation is dead: every callee receives a different, never-written frame slot. The checker's argument snapshots show fill pattern rather than the initialised words on the original side, confirming it.

Verified Two locator callees in the aim function are caller-cleanup (cdecl) despite the caller setting up a context register: the stack adjustment after the calls accounts for both pushes, so the callees pop nothing. Declaring them as callee-cleanup shifted the original's stack frame and corrupted every later frame read.

Verified The aim function's energy clamp is a floor at one, not a ceiling: the fall-through path of the comparison assigns. Misreading it scaled both drive outputs by the stored energy on exactly the affected trials.

Verified All four functions read at least one word they never wrote from their own stack frame; the checker pins these with a defined zero fill, recorded as narrowing in each result.

What was decided or recommended

  • Determine callee cleanup from the caller's stack adjustment, not from whether a context register is set; a wrong declaration silently shifts the original's frame.
  • Read fall-through versus taken arms of every comparison individually; two branches in this batch assigned on the fall-through side.
  • Consider folding exact per-word failure diffs into the stock checker driver; the truncated mismatch printout cost real debugging time twice.

How to reproduce it

Run the stock version 5 checker worker against this lane's four contracts and rewrite crate; each contract reproduces 1200 passing trials plus a caught wrong version. The dead descriptor shows as fill pattern in the callee argument snapshots of the configuration function's contract.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two early failures came from mistyped patch-site addresses (a dropped hex digit) and one from passing a relocated constant as a raw value. A relocation-audit script initially double-counted block addresses and wrongly reported zero relocations; it was fixed and cross-checked against the worker's own relocation behaviour.

A batch of 150 consecutive unnamed functions turned out to hold six different groups, and 145 of them got descriptive names. The most useful trick was reading pool-name strings out of pool constructors, which identified all seven entity pools at once.

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each function with a confidence level.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the memory-mapped image, collect direct calls, imports and memory references per function, resolve targets against the merged symbol and lane-name tables, and confirm pool identities from the pool constructor call sites.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The first evidence pass found only one string reference in the whole batch because the scanner only looked at immediate operands and missed all memory-disp references. A rescan with the correct operand type confirmed the batch genuinely has almost no string references. Caller attribution also misled several times by naming far-away native functions as callers when the true caller was an unnamed neighbour.

entry.title: Eight leaderboard row-fill functions verified; a reloc-script bug nearly deferred them all
entry.summary: All eight functions in this batch were verified against the stock checker with no failures over a thousand trials each, after two genuine rewrite bugs were found and fixed. The more useful finding is a tooling trap: a wrong handling of pefile relocation entries made the jump tables look unrelocated and the batch nearly got deferred for a checker gap that did not exist.
entry.content:
All eight functions in this batch were verified against the stock checker with no failures over a thousand trials each, after two genuine rewrite bugs were found and fixed. The more useful finding is a tooling trap: a wrong handling of pefile relocation entries made the jump tables look unrelocated and the batch nearly got deferred for a checker gap that did not exist.

What was asked

Rewrite eight medium-sized functions from the same template family in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, generating all eight from one script because they differ only in constants.

What was found

Verified The eight functions share identical logic with two parameters each: a leaderboard id constant and a row count (seven for one member, five for the rest). Each takes an object plus six stack words and returns a flag byte.

Verified Two subtle behaviours were confirmed by failing then passing trials: the function reports a stale stack-slot value, one iteration behind its cursor register, to one callee; and its key-length comparison is signed, so a negative length takes the copy path.

Verified A relocation check script added the page address twice because pefile reports each entry address already combined with its page. The corrected check shows every jump-table address in the batch is relocated, so the checker handles them normally.

What was decided or recommended

Future lanes should assert one known relocation entry before trusting any script that claims an address has none. Signedness of every comparison deserves its own audit pass: one signed greater-than among unsigned above-compares cost a full re-run here.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane generator to rebuild the eight rewrites and contracts, build the rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows, and run the stock checker driver over the eight contracts at a thousand trials each. All eight pass with their mutants caught.

What was confusing or went wrong

The wrong relocation result plus a plausible story about unrelocated reads made deferral look certain for about twenty minutes, until a probe showed most trials passing with correct dispatch. The probe data overruled the static analysis, and re-checking the script found the double-added page.

entry.title: Naming the follow cameras and the player ped
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three chase-camera classes, a camera probe-query family, shared camera math, and the player-ped class with its aim-target scanner; 143 of them are now named, most at medium confidence.

One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be three chase-camera classes, a camera probe-query family, shared camera math, and the player-ped class with its aim-target scanner; 143 of them are now named, most at medium confidence.

entry.title: Naming a 150-function run: cleanup tables, wanted state and three shared spans
entry.summary: One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the run exposed three reusable naming signals plus three inventory spans that hold more than one function.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-four of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the run exposed three reusable naming signals plus three inventory spans that hold more than one function.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name at high, medium or low confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and leaving the name empty where the behaviour cannot be told.

Verified The run splits into five groups: a single network socket helper, fragment and physics lifecycle code, mission cleanup and entity creation, the wanted level system, and interiors with the follow-vehicle camera.

Names follow the destructor convention already in the merged symbols, with a plain destructor body and a deleting wrapper variant. Later lanes should name tiny single-global functions by the global effect, distrust size-zero and gapfill entries until disassembled, and add batch addresses as enclosing anchors before mapping callers, or every caller misattributes to one distant function. Tail-call callees need collecting too: the jump-based evidence pass used here misses them.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image and confirm the mapping by decoding one known function first. Build one evidence table per function with direct calls, imports, string references, a caller scan and name lookups in the merged symbols, lane names and verified rewrites, then read the short functions and the leftovers directly. The lane scratch folder keeps the scripts and tables.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first caller map attributed most calls in the interiors group to one unrelated vtable function, because no nearby function starts were known; adding the batch addresses as anchors fixed it. A helper script named after a standard library module shadowed it and crashed on import until renamed. entry.title: Naming a run of ped physics and playstat functions
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named by behaviour: 133 got names and 17 were left empty as genuinely unknown. The batch turned out to be the ped ragdoll core, network stat registration, and the playstat submitter family.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions were named by behaviour: 133 got names and 17 were left empty as genuinely unknown. The batch turned out to be the ped ragdoll core, network stat registration, and the playstat submitter family.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with a confidence for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from evidence, strongest first: referenced strings, called imports, known callers and classes, then behaviour.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three groups: about a hundred ped physics and ragdoll methods, about a dozen network stat registration routines, and about thirty playstat submitters and accessors.

Verified The key that unlocked the ped group is a four-field model: the active physics instance pointer, the normal instance, the ragdoll instance, and a small ragdoll-state value. Dozens of functions test whether the active pointer equals the ragdoll one and switch between the two, which made the enter, exit, link and state names fall out directly.

Verified The health setter stores its value with three threshold flags against shared constants that read back as exactly fifty and one hundred, plus a non-positive flag.

Verified Three network routines are straight-line siblings that each register eight stats with defaults and then run an achievement check; they differ only in the stat id sets and the check slot.

Verified Every playstat class has a matched pair: one virtual slot writes the stat into a message and the other reads it back, confirmed by the verified rewrite notes and by publish-flavoured callees on one side and parse-flavoured callees on the other.

Inferred A neighbouring routine labelled as a playstat destructor is actually a timer-driven flush driver: it compares pending arrays against committed ones on tick intervals and submits what changed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Seventeen functions were left unnamed with low confidence rather than guessed, including a health-setter twin whose extra argument is never read and an entity flag setter shared by nineteen classes whose bit meaning is unknown.
  • Three inventory entries merge two or three functions into one size, and one gapfill entry jumps backward out of its own bounds; the queue should re-split them before production lanes take them.
  • The most reusable naming signals for the next lane are: native-implementation callers pin small setters, physics constructor callees reveal setup routines, and the ragdoll four-field model names a whole family at once.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: direct-call targets resolved against verified rewrites and lane names, import calls, string references, and caller sites found by scanning for relative calls and resolved to enclosing named functions. Read every small function fully, then the table-unclear ones, then name from the strongest signal.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two virtual slots do exactly the same thing with different arity, and two minimised-window-gated routines look important but their roles stayed unclear; all four were left empty. A first attempt to confirm an entity flag bit against a public SDK failed on a wrong file path and was abandoned as not worth more time. The shared constants table reads back neighbouring values alongside the target, so each constant had to be read individually rather than trusted from context.

entry.title: A call argument that changes on every run
entry.summary: Verified A function that passes a relocated address to a callee cannot have that argument compared exactly, because the checker's run of the original sits at a different base address in every worker process while the rewrite's value stays fixed. The fix is to skip that one argument and say so, after proving everything else matches.
entry.content:
Verified A function that passes a relocated address to a callee cannot have that argument compared exactly, because the checker's run of the original sits at a different base address in every worker process while the rewrite's value stays fixed. The fix is to skip that one argument and say so, after proving everything else matches.

What was asked

Routine production work: rewrite six neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each against the original with the differential checker.

What was found

Verified One function builds a table pointer from a file constant and passes it to a calibration call. The constant carries a relocation entry, so the worker patches it for wherever it placed that run's copy of the code. Two runs of the same contract, minutes apart, logged two different raw values for that argument (heap and everything else identical), which rules out nondeterminism in the function and points at the mapping base moving per worker.

Verified Unrelocated reads are unaffected: constants and zero data read through plain absolute addresses returned identical file bytes across thousands of trials and several workers, so only relocated operands need this treatment.

Inferred The logged form of the same address can also differ between the two sides (region-relative on the original side, raw on the rewrite side), which looks like a second problem but is only display: skipping the argument removes both.

What was decided or recommended

  • Skip a call argument that carries a relocated address (call_skip), and record it in the narrowed list with the reason. The skipped value in this case was still pinned down three other ways (a second call argument, a table lookup, a stored rate), so the proof lost almost nothing.
  • Do not use a bit mask to dodge it: a mask still compares values, and the values legitimately differ across runs.
  • Suspect this whenever the calls check alone fails with two different raw hex values on consecutive runs while heap, stack and return value stay green.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract whose original passes a relocated address on to a call. Run it twice and compare the logged call arguments in the two verdicts: the address argument differs while all other comparisons pass. Adding the argument to call_skip turns both runs green.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first attempt at this function also had a real rewrite bug (a matrix result subtracted instead of stored), which failed heap and calls together and hid the mapping issue until the rewrite was fixed. The region-relative versus raw display then sent the diagnosis toward the pointer comparison before the second run showed the values themselves moving. Both misdirections cost about ten minutes.

Read the executable through the mapped image, disassemble each batch function, resolve direct calls and string references against the merged symbol files and verified rewrites, match stamped vtables against the class structure files, and map pool headers from the setup code in the initialiser.
